verdict.rationale: Direct queries confirm the canon affirms angelic protective ministry to God's people, but it does not lexically lock down a one-to-one assignment of a specific angel to a specific believer. Hebrews 1:14 predicates angels collectively as ministering spirits (leitourgika pneumata) sent for service (eis diakonian) for the plural those about to inherit salvation (tous mellontas kleronomein soterian), and Matthew 18:10 places their angels (hoi angeloi auton) in genitive plural (the 'from-X' grammatical form, plural) agreement with the plural class of these little ones (ton mikron touton). The only singular his angel (ho angelos autou) applied to a believer is Acts 12:15, voiced as reported speech of the gathered church (V-IAI-3P elegon, meaning 'they kept saying') inside indirect discourse, while every other his angel (ho angelos autou) pattern in the canon refers to God's or the Lord's angel. Psalm 91:11 commissions plural his angels (malakaw) to guard one addressee, and Psalm 34:7 reverses that to one angel of the LORD (malak YHWH) around a plural group of those who fear him. The vocabulary supports angelic ministry as a class fact, but it does not force, nor exclude, dedicated personal assignment, which is the lexical reason the proposition is disputed.

scripture.force: God will command (yetsavveh, in the Hebrew intensive form, ongoing or repeated past action used here as future, third person masculine singular) his angels (malakaw, masculine plural noun with 'his' suffix referring to God) to guard you (lishmarka, the simple active form of the Hebrew verb in infinitive construct with 'your' singular suffix) in all your ways. The construction is plural commissioning agents protecting one singular addressee, which establishes angelic protection of an individual as a class fact but does not pin one specific named angel to that person. The grammar leaves the assignment open: many angels could be commissioned to one person, or the same angels could rotate, or one could be dedicated.

The rhetorical question predicates all of them (pantes, adjective nominative plural masculine, meaning 'all') as ministering spirits (leitourgika pneumata, neuter nominative plural, a phrase whose adjective leitourgikos is a hapax, that is, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, Strong's G3010) being sent out (apostellomena, present passive participle, meaning continuously being sent out) for service (eis diakonian) on behalf of those about to inherit salvation (tous mellontas kleronomein soterian, plural accusative, the 'direct-object' grammatical form). Every grammatical handle is plural to plural with a present-tense iterative aspect (an ongoing, repeated action), so the verse grounds angelic ministry to the saved as an ongoing class fact while supplying no individualizing distribution.

Their angels (hoi angeloi auton, nominative plural subject, the 'subject' grammatical form) of these little ones (ton mikron touton, genitive plural, the 'from-X' grammatical form) always (dia pantos) see continuously (blepousi, V-PAI-3P, present active indicative third person plural, ongoing simple statement of fact) the face of my Father in heaven. The pronoun 'their' (auton) is P-GPN, that is, pronoun in the genitive plural neuter form, agreeing with the plural class of little ones, so on plain morphology the verse pairs a plurality of angels with a plurality of little ones. A strict distributive reading (one angel per little one) is grammatically possible but not required by the plural-to-plural agreement, which is the lexical seat of the dispute.

It is his angel (ho angelos estin autou, singular nominative the angel, V-PAI-3S estin meaning 'is' as an ongoing simple statement of fact, P-GSM autou meaning 'his' in singular genitive masculine, the 'of-him' grammatical form) is the only canon instance where singular 'angel' (angelos) plus singular 'his' refers to a human believer rather than to God's angel. But the clause is reported speech inside indirect discourse: the narrator says they kept saying (elegon, V-IAI-3P, imperfect active indicative third person plural, ongoing or repeated past action) when Rhoda kept insisting (diischyrizeto, V-INI-3S, imperfect middle indicative third person singular) it was Peter. The verse records what the gathered believers assumed, not what the narrator affirms. Every other canonical his angel (ho angelos autou) phrase (Matthew 1:20, Matthew 28:2, Luke 1:13, Acts 12:7, Acts 12:11, Revelation 1:1, Revelation 22:6, and so on) refers to God's or the Lord's angel, not a believer's personal angel, so even the lexical pattern of the phrase itself runs against personalizing it here.

The angel of the LORD (malak YHWH, singular construct meaning 'angel of YHWH') encamps around those who fear him (lirea'aw, plural) and rescues them. The distribution is reversed from Psalm 91:11: one angel for many beneficiaries. Read together with Psalm 91:11 (many angels for one addressee), the canon clearly does not standardize a one-to-one mapping, which is the textual reason the dedicated personal-guardian thesis cannot be straightforwardly derived from the protective vocabulary.

The prince of the kingdom of Persia (sar malkut Paras, where sar means 'prince' or 'chief') is named, then Michael, one of the chief princes (echad hasarim harishonim), comes to help. The construction pairs angelic figures with nations and kingdoms, not with individual believers. Daniel 12:1 extends this: Michael is the great prince who stands over the sons of your people (hasar haggadol ha'omed al bnei ammeka). The Daniel canon supplies an angels-over-collectives pattern (nations, peoples) rather than angels-over-individuals.

The angel who redeems me from all evil (hammalak hagga'el oti mikkol ra') is Jacob's singular protective angel, applied personally with the definite article 'the' and a relative participle. The context, however, is the Angel of YHWH motif that functions as a christophany (a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ) or theophany (an appearance of God himself) in the Pentateuch (the first five books of the Bible), not a separate created guardian, so as evidence for a personal created guardian angel per believer it is structurally ambiguous: the same figure who blesses Jacob's children is identified with the One whose name is invoked over them.

complicating_texts.resolution: The genitive plural 'their' (auton, the 'from-X' grammatical form in plural) agrees with the plural class of these little ones (ton mikron touton), so plural-to-plural agreement is the default reading and a strict distributive one-angel-per-little-one reading is admissible but not required. The lexical pattern by itself neither establishes nor excludes individualized assignment.

It is his angel (ho angelos estin autou) is grammatically the strongest individualizing datum in the canon, but it sits inside reported speech (they kept saying, elegon, V-IAI-3P, imperfect active indicative third person plural, ongoing or repeated past action) of the gathered believers, not in narrator-asserted exposition. Combined with the fact that every other his angel (ho angelos autou) phrase in the canon refers to God's angel rather than a believer's, the verse attests that a personal-angel belief existed in the first-century church without elevating it to doctrinal assertion.

Plural neuter spirits (pneumata) plus plural masculine accusative those about to (tous mellontas) leaves no individualizing slot in the syntax. The verse strongly grounds ongoing angelic ministry to the saved as a class but provides no lexical handle for one-to-one assignment, so it is consistent with either lens without favoring either.

Singular angel of the LORD (malak YHWH) for plural fearers reverses the Psalm 91:11 distribution and confirms that the canon does not normalize a uniform one-to-one mapping. This text by itself does not refute personal guardianship; it shows the protective lexicon ranges freely over one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many configurations.

Angels-over-nations vocabulary (prince, sar, of Persia, Michael over the sons of your people, bnei ammeka) shows another canonical pattern where angelic agents are paired with collectives rather than individuals. It does not refute the personal-angel thesis but it does refute any claim that the Bible knows only an individual-pairing pattern.

The Jacobic singular the angel who redeems me (hammalak hagga'el oti) looks like the strongest Old Testament support for personal protective angels, but the Angel-of-YHWH motif in the Pentateuch (the first five books of the Bible) standardly functions as a theophany (an appearance of God himself) rather than a created guardian, and the lexical data alone cannot fully disambiguate the two referents in this verse. The ambiguity is left flagged rather than forced to a resolution.

variants.note: Matthew 18:10 carries a known editorial marker on 'in heaven' (en ouranois) at the end of the verse and Acts 12:15 carries a marker on the verb of being, but the witnesses agree on their angels (hoi angeloi auton) in Matthew 18:10 and on it is his angel (ho angelos estin autou) in Acts 12:15, so the disputed status of personal guardianship is unaffected by any plausible variant. The bundle reports not_in_ecm_scope true and supplies no variant units, so no CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, a statistical technique for analyzing manuscript relationships) analysis was performed.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Angels protect and serve God's people as a class; the canon does not lexically require one-to-one assignment.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Psalm 91:11 uses plural angels for one addressee, Psalm 34:7 uses one angel of the LORD (malak YHWH) for plural fearers, Hebrews 1:14 has plural ministering spirits (leitourgika pneumata) for plural heirs, and Matthew 18:10 places plural angels with the plural class of little ones. The only singular his angel for a believer (Acts 12:15) is reported speech, not narrator assertion. The economical synthesis is class-level ministry with no fixed personal pairing required.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: A specific angel is associated with the individual believer; Acts 12:15 and a distributive reading of Matt 18:10 anchor this canonical pattern.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: It is his angel (ho angelos estin autou, singular angel, singular his) about Peter is a grammatically clean individualizing phrase, even granting it is reported speech of the gathered church. A distributive reading of their angels (hoi angeloi auton) in Matthew 18:10 (one angel per little one) is grammatically possible and coheres with the gravity Jesus attaches to despising the little ones. Read this way, the canonical pattern is real even if not explicit, and the personal-guardian reading is a permissible inference.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Gen 48:16 hammalak hagga'el oti is not evidence for created personal guardians at all, because the Angel of YHWH in the Pentateuch is a theophanic figure.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The same angel (malak) who redeems Jacob in Genesis 48:16 is identified with God in Genesis 31:11-13 and Exodus 3:2-6, and Jacob asks him to bless the boys in language proper to YHWH. So Genesis 48:16 belongs to a different lexical track than created-angel guardianship, which means it should be removed from the support stack for personal guardian angels rather than counted toward it.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Daniel locates angelic agency at the level of peoples and kingdoms rather than individuals, so any general lexical pattern is at least as well supported for collectives as for individuals.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The prince of the kingdom of Persia (sar malkut Paras) and Michael, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people (Michael hasar haggadol ha'omed al bnei ammeka), show angels assigned to nations and peoples. This pattern is structurally analogous to the personal-guardian thesis (one named angel responsible for one group) but it is collective. The lexical record supplies the analog at the collective level explicitly and at the individual level only by inference.

hermeneutics.notes: All four lenses are derivable from the same Hebrew and Greek vocabulary without contradiction. The disputed status of the proposition reflects this fan of admissible lexical patterns, not a single ambiguous word or a single ambiguous clause. The analogia scripturae (the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture) harmonizes everything under general angelic ministry but cannot rank the personal-versus-collective distribution from the vocabulary alone.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: A specific angel is dedicated to each individual believer for ongoing personal protection and ministry.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem embeds a meta judgment (permissible but not dogmatically required) which a lexical store cannot adjudicate because permissibility and dogmatic status are ecclesial categories, not lexical facts. The verdict is therefore derived on the underlying lexical claim that the cited texts teach a dedicated one-to-one assignment of an angel to a believer, and the lexical data leave that claim contested rather than entailed.

lay_summary: Six anchor passages bear on whether each believer has a personal guardian angel, and the words distribute the relationship in several different ways. Psalm 91:11 says God will command his angels (malakaw), in the plural, to guard you, in the singular, so many agents are commissioned to protect one person. Psalm 34:7 reverses that: the angel of the LORD (malak YHWH), in the singular, encamps around those who fear him, in the plural. Hebrews 1:14 calls angels (angeloi) in the plural ministering spirits (leitourgika pneumata) sent out for service (eis diakonian) for those, in the plural, who are about to inherit salvation, with every grammatical handle plural to plural. Matthew 18:10 says the angels (angeloi), plural, of these little ones, plural, always see the Father's face, and the 'their' (auton) attaches to the plural class, so the default reading is plural to plural rather than one angel per child. Acts 12:15 supplies the one place in the New Testament where a singular his angel (ho angelos autou) is applied to a believer, when the gathered church says about Peter at the door, it is his angel, but the writer reports this as what the believers kept saying, not as his own assertion, and every other singular his angel phrase in the canon refers to God's angel, not a believer's. Daniel 10 and 12 add angels associated with nations and peoples rather than individuals (the prince, sar, of Persia, and Michael over the sons of your people, bnei ammeka). Genesis 48:16 has Jacob speak of the singular angel (hammalak) who redeemed him, which sounds personal, but the same figure functions elsewhere as a manifestation of God himself. Put together, the words clearly affirm that angels protect and serve God's people, in many configurations: one to many, many to one, one to a nation, many to a class. They do not lock in one fixed pattern of one specific angel assigned to one specific believer, and the only clearly individualizing phrase is reported speech rather than doctrine. That is why a careful reader can defend either a collective-ministry view or a personal-guardian view from the same vocabulary, and why the proposition lands as lexically disputed.
